verdict: Avoid new plywood, veneer and laminate exposure in Tinsukia; lend only to established, timber-linked units with tight monthly stock and receivable control.
title: Tinsukia plywood, veneer & laminates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A plywood or veneer unit buys face veneer, core timber and chemicals, peels and presses them into boards, and sells through dealers into housing and interior demand.** Cash is locked in the timber and veneer yard and in dealer credit, not in the press. Ratings flag input price volatility and import dependence in select timber as the core risk [8], and Greenply's own rating stresses that plants sit near the raw material source for competitive cost [10]. So when a proposal lands, check where the log and veneer yard is relative to the unit; if timber is trucked in from another state, ask for the landed cost per unit and the supplier list.

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is weak: Assam electricity demand is up only 1.9% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, 7.6 pp slower [D].** India-wide output is down 0.8% Apr-to-date while bank credit is up 20.6% YoY, a 21.4 pp gap [D], and the repo is 5.5% with a tightening stance [D]. That combination means borrowed money is chasing flat output. The Tinsukia news is thin: a ₹55-crore AAC block plant was inaugurated and ₹3 lakh crore of Assam commitments are at implementation stage [1], but nothing there is plywood-specific. A local post claims illegal sand dumping will make 'polokh' maati pricier [2] — treat it as unverified chatter, not a cost line.

## Where the growth is
**Peer results show the split clearly: plywood and veneer are growing while commodity laminates lag.** Greenlam's plywood segment grew 90.7% YoY in Q4FY25 [4] and 22.2% YoY in Q2FY26 [6], while laminates volume fell 7% YoY in Q1FY27 [5]. Pursue established veneer and plywood units with own or tied timber supply, and branded laminate players with dealer pull. Avoid traders who buy and resell boards, and new laminate capacity in the commoditised grade [8].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock statements and a charge on the timber and veneer yard; set the drawing power on paid stock, not book debt. Ask for monthly sales and receivable-age data — collect from customer where the current cycle length is not on file. Peer margin pressure came from chemicals and resin costs [7], so covenant that any chemical cost pass-through is evidenced in invoices.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the yard, not the P&L.** Falling veneer stock against flat sales means the unit is selling raw material to fund losses. Rising dealer receivables beyond the agreed cycle, or a shift to cash sales at a discount, signals pricing stress.
